preguntas.pregunta: A clinic is choosing between two safety winged-steel needles. Which feature matches what is recommended for a device with a safety mechanism?
opciones: The shield is part of the device and stays protective all the way to disposal
The shield is added by the user after the needle leaves the patient's vein
The shield can be switched off when the phlebotomist needs to reuse the holder
The shield is activated with two hands, one on each side of the exposed tip
preguntas.explicacion: The list of desirable characteristics is short and demanding: no needle at all where that is possible; a safety feature built into the device rather than added on; passive operation if it can be had; a feature the user can see is engaged; one that cannot be switched off and keeps protecting through disposal; and a device that is reliable, practical and safe for the patient. Cortisol requires a 12-hour fast, which the run interrupted

preguntas.pregunta: An erythrocyte sedimentation rate rack stands on a bench beside a centrifuge, leaning a few degrees off the vertical. What does that do to the result?
opciones: The rate rises, and a tilt of only 3° can add as much as 30 % to it
The rate falls, because tilted red cells settle against the tube wall
The rate is unchanged, since the reading is corrected for the angle
The rate rises, but only when the tube was also underfilled at collection
preguntas.explicacion: Technical conditions move this test more than most. A tube tilted 3° from the vertical can raise the value by as much as 30 %, and vibration from nearby equipment raises it too. A warm room lowers blood viscosity and pushes the rate up, and direct sunlight also raises it. Underfilling adds air bubbles, which lift the reading as well, so the rack belongs upright, still and out of the sun.

Pressure was kept up too long after the needle had come out

preguntas.pregunta: A vaccinated phlebotomist with a documented anti-HBs level of 10 mIU/mL or more is exposed to an HBsAg-positive patient. What does the CDC recommend?

One dose of HBIG plus a vaccine booster, then anti-HBs testing 1 to 2 months afterward
Two doses of HBIG one month apart, since vaccinated workers cannot be revaccinated
A repeat anti-HBs test now, with HBIG only if the level has fallen below 10 mIU/mL

preguntas.pregunta: A phlebotomist cleans the antecubital site with an alcohol-containing disinfectant and, to save time, inserts the needle while the skin is still wet. Why does the CDC object?
opciones: The disinfectant has to dry on the skin before the culture is drawn

Alcohol is only for the bottle septum, never for the venipuncture site
preguntas.explicacion: For blood cultures the skin is disinfected with an alcohol-containing product and allowed to dry before the draw; improper antisepsis is a recognised cause of contamination. preguntas.pregunta: A new phlebotomist says she was vaccinated against hepatitis B as a child but has no records. How does the CDC treat her?
opciones: As unvaccinated: only written, dated records count, so she should complete the series
As vaccinated: a single anti-HBs test of 10 mIU/mL or more proves immunity
As vaccinated: childhood vaccination is routine and needs no post-vaccination testing
As a non-responder: she should receive HBIG at hire and be tested every year
preguntas.explicacion: Only written, dated records count as evidence of hepatitis B vaccination, so clinicians who cannot document three doses are considered unvaccinated and should complete the series, with anti-HBs tested 1 to 2 months after the third dose. An anti-HBs of 10 mIU/mL or more is a reliable marker of protection only when testing follows a documented three-dose series, so a lone test in someone without records should not be read as immunity. Facilities are encouraged to look for old records and enter doses in the state immunization system.

preguntas.pregunta: Which password practice is consistent with HIPAA security guidance?
opciones: Unique passwords for each user, never shared, written down or emailed
A single department password changed each year at annual training
Passwords posted near the workstation so that coverage staff can log in quickly
Passwords of consecutive digits, which are easier to audit
preguntas.explicacion: Every worker who accesses patient records needs a unique, strong password that mixes letters, numbers and symbols, is changed periodically, is never shared, verbalized, written down near the computer or emailed, and is not built from consecutive digits or easily guessed information; the IT department checks password quality before granting access. Only the mother's name and hospital number; the rest is added by the state laboratory
The infant's blood type and Apgar score, which the laboratory needs to interpret results
The date and time of collection only; identity details are added once the spots have dried

preguntas.pregunta: A skin puncture must supply a haematology specimen, a chemistry specimen and a blood bank specimen. In what order are they collected?
opciones: Haematology, then chemistry, then blood bank
Blood bank, then chemistry, then haematology
Chemistry, then haematology, then blood bank
Blood bank, then haematology, then chemistry
preguntas.explicacion: With skin punctures the haematology specimen is collected first, followed by the chemistry and blood bank specimens, an order that is essential to minimize the effects of platelet clumping. It is the reverse of the order used for venepuncture. If more than two specimens are needed, venepuncture may give more accurate results.

preguntas.pregunta: A patient files a privacy complaint against a clinic. What does HIPAA say about how the clinic may respond?
opciones: It may not intimidate or retaliate against the patient for filing the complaint
It may decline further treatment, since the relationship of trust has been broken
It may require the patient to waive the complaint as a condition of care
It may share the complaint with other providers so they are warned
preguntas.explicacion: Section 164.530(g) forbids a covered entity from intimidating, threatening, coercing, discriminating against or retaliating against any individual for exercising a right under the rule or taking part in any of its processes, including filing a complaint, and 164.530(h) forbids requiring individuals to waive their rights as a condition of treatment, payment, enrollment or benefits. The entity must have its own complaint process, document complaints and their disposition, and mitigate any harm from a violation. Sharing the complaint with other providers would itself be an unpermitted disclosure.

preguntas.pregunta: A phenytoin level is ordered and the phlebotomist draws it into a serum separator tube with gel. Why will the laboratory not accept that tube for therapeutic drug monitoring?
opciones: The barrier gel can absorb drugs such as phenytoin, phenobarbital, lidocaine and carbamazepine
The clot activator in the gel tube breaks down phenytoin before the serum can be separated
The gel prevents the sample from being carried on ice and in the dark as drug levels require
The gel tube cannot be centrifuged, and drug assays are run only on centrifuged specimens
preguntas.explicacion: For therapeutic drug monitoring the laboratory refuses tubes with serum separator gel because the barrier gel can absorb some drugs, phenytoin, phenobarbital, lidocaine and carbamazepine among them, which was shown by recovering the drugs from the gel after extraction with methanol; standard tubes without gel are suggested instead. Ice and darkness are the rule for methotrexate, not a property of the tube.

preguntas.pregunta: During a draw, an evacuated tube that was briefly uncapped earlier is pushed onto the needle and no blood enters it. What is the likely cause?

The anticoagulant was missing from the tube during packaging
The needle bevel is lying against the wall of the vein
The tube was drawn out of sequence and its additive was spent
preguntas.explicacion: Among the issues of concern, the review notes that tubes can be damaged and that the vacuum can be lost when a tube is uncapped; without vacuum the tube cannot pull blood. preguntas.pregunta: A 16 G needle is used on a small forearm vein and a large haematoma forms. According to WHO Chapter 3, what is the effect of a needle that is too large, and of one that is too small?
opciones: Too large tears the vein and causes bleeding; too small damages the cells and invalidates whole-cell tests
Too large damages the blood cells and invalidates the tests; too small tears the vein and causes a haematoma
Too large slows the draw so the sample clots in the tube; too small lets air into the tubing of the set
Too large causes haemoconcentration of the sample; too small causes the tube to lose its vacuum early
preguntas.explicacion: Section 3.1.1 says that a needle too large for the vein will tear it and cause bleeding, a haematoma, while a needle too small will damage the blood cells during sampling and invalidate tests that need whole cells, haemoglobin or free plasma. preguntas.pregunta: A donor refuses to put their initials on the tamper-evident seals of the two bottles. What is the consequence?
opciones: It is noted on the remarks line and the collection is completed as usual
It is recorded as a refusal to test and the urine is discarded at once
The collector initials the seals instead and the specimen goes out normally
A second collection is done under direct observation with new bottles
preguntas.explicacion: The donor is asked to initial each label or seal, but a failure or a refusal to do so is noted on the remarks line of the chain of custody form and the collection is finished; it is not treated as a refusal to test. Refusing to give donor information or to sign the certification statement is handled the same way. What does count as a refusal is leaving before the process ends or refusing a second attempt.

preguntas.pregunta: Which two practices are forbidden once a sharps container is in service?
opciones: Overfilling it, and emptying its contents out to use it again
Sealing it with a lid, and moving it closer to the drawing chair
Labelling it, and keeping it within arm's reach of the worker
Overfilling it, and sealing it before it has been fully filled
preguntas.explicacion: The container is sealed with a tamper-proof lid, and the two things not to do are overfilling it and decanting it. Keeping it within arm's reach and clearly visible is the correct practice, since the used device is meant to go in immediately rather than travel across the room.

preguntas.pregunta: A phlebotomist finds the sharps container at her station filled to the marked line. What does the standard require before it is carried away?
opciones: Close it immediately before removal, and use a second closable container if leakage is possible
Press the contents down so the lid will close, then carry it to the soiled utility room
Open the lid and tip the sharps into a red bag that is closed before it is removed
Leave it in place until the end of the shift, the deadline set for contaminated surfaces
preguntas.explicacion: Paragraph (d)(4)(iii)(A)(3) covers the moment a sharps container leaves the area where it was used: the lid goes on first, so nothing can spill or poke out while it is handled, and if the container could leak it travels inside a second one that closes, holds everything and carries the label or the color code. Paragraph (A)(2) already required the container to be replaced routinely and never allowed to overfill, so pressing the contents down is the opposite of the rule, and (A)(4) forbids opening or emptying a reusable container by hand. The end-of-shift deadline belongs to work surfaces in (d)(4)(ii)(A).

preguntas.pregunta: What is gained by teaching a patient to recognize the warning signs of a faint?
opciones: The faint is often prevented and the risk of a traumatic fall drops
The faint is shortened, although the risk of a traumatic fall is unchanged
The blood pressure stays high enough for the draw to be completed
The pulse rate rises enough that the tourniquet may be left in place
preguntas.explicacion: Knowing the symptoms often prevents the episode outright and reduces the risk of a traumatic fall, because the patient lies down before consciousness goes. That is the practical reason for asking, before a draw, whether the person has ever fainted during an injection or a blood test.

preguntas.pregunta: How often must a nonwaived laboratory perform calibration verification, and what materials does it use?
opciones: At least every 6 months, with a low or zero, a mid-point and a high value near the top of the range
At least every 12 months, with two control materials of different concentrations run in duplicate
Only when a control fails, with a calibrator from the same lot that was used to calibrate the system
Each day of testing, with a single calibrator traceable to a certified reference material
preguntas.explicacion: Calibration verification confirms the system is still accurate across its reportable range. It is done at least once every 6 months and also after a complete reagent change, after major maintenance or replacement of critical parts, when controls show an unusual trend or fall outside limits that other corrective steps cannot fix, and whenever the laboratory's own schedule calls for it. Materials cover a minimal, a mid-point and a maximum value.

preguntas.pregunta: What color and legend does OSHA require on a biohazard warning label?
opciones: Fluorescent orange or orange-red, with the biohazard symbol and legend in a contrasting color
Bright yellow with a black skull and crossbones, the GHS pictogram for acute toxicity
Red with white lettering, matching the red bags that may replace the label
Fluorescent orange-red with a black frame set on a point, as on chemical labels
preguntas.explicacion: Paragraph (g)(1)(i)(B) and (C) require the BIOHAZARD legend and symbol on labels that are fluorescent orange or orange-red, or predominantly so, with lettering and symbols in a contrasting color, affixed so they cannot be lost or removed by accident. Red bags or containers may substitute for the label under (g)(1)(i)(E), but the label itself is not specified as red with white text. The skull and crossbones and the red square frame set on a point are elements of Hazard Communication chemical labels, not of the bloodborne pathogens standard.

preguntas.pregunta: In the three-step assessment of an occupational HIV exposure, what does the first step establish?
opciones: Whether an infectious fluid was involved, and by which route and how severe
Whether the source patient is on treatment and what the viral load is
Whether prophylaxis is indicated or observation alone is enough
Whether the worker completed the hepatitis B vaccine series
preguntas.explicacion: The three steps run in order. First comes the exposure itself: was blood, another infectious body fluid, or an instrument contaminated with blood involved, and if so by what route and how badly. Contact with intact skin carries no meaningful risk; for a mucous membrane the volume and duration count; for a percutaneous injury it matters whether the needle was solid or hollow-bore and whether it had been in a vein or artery. The source patient's status is the second step, and the decision on prophylaxis the third.
preguntas.fuente: StatPearls, "Needlestick", Evaluation: CDC 3-Step Risk Assessment

preguntas.pregunta: A patient mentions she is thinking of stopping a medicine, and the phlebotomist tells her what to do. Which pitfall is that?
opciones: Unsolicited advice, which can feel intrusive and unempathetic
Providing false reassurance, which can rupture the relationship
Changing the subject abruptly, which can come across as dismissive
Responding defensively, which closes off the patient's own view
preguntas.explicacion: Advice the patient never asked for lands as intrusive and lacking in empathy, unless they have expressly asked to be advised. False reassurance risks a severe rupture in the relationship, above all when the desired outcome is not achieved; an abrupt change of subject can be perceived as dismissive; and a defensive answer leaves the patient no room to express frustration.

preguntas.pregunta: Under 42 CFR 482.13(d), how may a hospital patient request access to their own medical records?
opciones: By oral or written request, in the format requested if readily producible
Only by written request notarized and signed by the attending physician
Only through an attorney, since records are hospital property
Only after discharge, once the record has been completed and coded
preguntas.explicacion: The confidentiality standard gives the patient the right to access their medical records, including current records, upon an oral or written request, in the form and format requested when readily producible, electronic included, or otherwise in a readable hard copy or an agreed format, within a reasonable time; the hospital may not frustrate legitimate efforts to obtain records and must meet requests as quickly as its record system permits. The same standard protects the confidentiality of clinical records and, separately, the right to personal privacy and care in a safe setting.

preguntas.pregunta: What does 'gender identity' mean?
opciones: One's own sense of gender, matching or differing from the sex assigned at birth
The appearance, dress, mannerisms and speech associated with femininity or masculinity
The sex recorded for an infant on the basis of the external genitalia
The gender that an observer assigns to a person on first meeting them

preguntas.pregunta: In published studies of laboratory errors, which phase of the total testing process consistently accounts for more than half of all errors?
opciones: The pre-analytical phase
The analytical phase
The post-analytical phase
The post-post-analytical phase
preguntas.explicacion: The two extra-analytical phases together carry four to five times the errors of the analytical phase, and the pre-analytical phase alone represents over half of all errors in the published series; an Italian stat laboratory found 62 % pre-analytical, 15 % analytical and 23 % post-analytical in both 1996 and 2006. The analytical phase, by contrast, performs close to 5 sigma.

preguntas.pregunta: A blind patient needs to review the consent information. Which ADA auxiliary aid fits?
opciones: A qualified reader, large print, or Braille
A qualified sign language interpreter or captioning
A qualified speech-to-speech transliterator
A companion who reads and signs the form for him
preguntas.explicacion: For people who are blind or have vision loss, the ADA's auxiliary aids include a qualified reader, large print, Braille, an accessible electronic file for a screen reader, or an audio recording. Interpreters and real-time captioning are aids for people who are deaf, and speech-to-speech transliteration serves speech disabilities. Braille works only for those who read it, so the person's own method matters.

preguntas.pregunta: How should a phlebotomist decide how to address an older patient?
opciones: Default to formal terms such as Mr. or Ms., and ask how they prefer to be addressed
Use first names, which feel warmer to most older adults than formal titles
Use affectionate terms such as 'dear' to put the patient at ease quickly
Use the name the companion uses for the patient during the visit
preguntas.explicacion: Speak to the patient as a fellow adult and establish respect by using formal language as the default, such as Mr. or Ms., and avoid familiar terms like 'dear', which can be perceived as disrespectful; staff can also check with patients about the form of address they prefer. Older people may be used to more formal terms of address.

preguntas.pregunta: A dried blood spot is visibly smaller than its printed circle. What does this tell the laboratory?
opciones: That total spot volume is well below the 75 to 100 µL target, so punches may hold too little
That the newborn's hematocrit was high, because hematocrit is the main driver of the spot's diameter
That the spot dried too fast, which shrinks the paper fibres and the visible stain
That the collector used the second drop, which spreads less than the first
preguntas.explicacion: Spot diameter is greatly influenced by total spot volume and not highly influenced by hematocrit, so a spot smaller than the printed circle signals a volume substantially below the 75 to 100 µL target and punches whose volume may fall outside the acceptable range. Hematocrit shows instead in the edges: lower-hematocrit spots have smoother borders, higher ones more irregular.

preguntas.pregunta: A phlebotomist is stuck with a needle used on a patient known to have hepatitis C. What does the CDC say about prophylaxis?
opciones: No vaccine and no recommended PEP exist; follow-up testing finds infection early so it can be treated
Immune globulin is given within 24 hours, followed by baseline and 6-month antibody tests
A 28-day antiviral course is started within 72 hours, as for HIV
A single dose of vaccine plus HBIG is given if the worker's antibody level is under 10 mIU/mL
preguntas.explicacion: There is no vaccine against hepatitis C and no post-exposure treatment that prevents infection; neither immune globulin nor antiviral therapy is recommended after exposure. The 2020 guidance does not recommend routine HCV PEP with direct-acting antivirals, noting a percutaneous transmission risk of about 0.2 percent, and instead sets a testing schedule so that infection is detected and treated early. Immune globulin and HBIG with vaccine are hepatitis B measures; the 28-day course within 72 hours is HIV PEP.
preguntas.fuente: CDC, Exposure to Blood: What Healthcare Personnel Need to Know (2003), Treatment for the Exposure: HCV; CDC, Guidelines for Health Care Personnel Exposed to Hepatitis C Virus, HCV postexposure prophylaxis

preguntas.pregunta: Which practices are current ways to reduce iatrogenic blood loss in neonates?
opciones: Placental blood for admission tests, microtiter tubes, and laboratory analyzers that need less sample
Larger single draws once a day, standard tubes filled to the line, and weekly transfusion
Arterial sampling only, heparinized syringes, and discarding the first 2 mL of each line draw
Capillary sampling for every test, adhesive strips, and iron supplementation from day one
preguntas.explicacion: Current practices include placental blood for admission laboratory testing, microtiter tubes for specimen collection and sophisticated laboratory analyzers, although clinician ordering remains the major driver of loss. Closed devices that return line-flush blood, which cut loss by about 25% in NICU and adult ICU patients, and small-volume tubes that may reduce anemia risk.

The name of the courier and the vehicle used

preguntas.pregunta: The grey top tube holds two substances. Which one is the anticoagulant, and what does the other one do?
opciones: Potassium oxalate binds calcium; sodium fluoride blocks glycolysis
Sodium fluoride binds the calcium; potassium oxalate blocks glycolysis
Sodium citrate binds calcium; sodium fluoride preserves the cells
Potassium oxalate inhibits thrombin; sodium fluoride binds calcium
preguntas.explicacion: The grey tube contains potassium oxalate, which binds calcium and so prevents coagulation, together with sodium fluoride, which acts as an antiglycolytic agent; that combination is why the tube is used for plasma glucose and lactic acid. Swapping the two roles reverses the review, citrate belongs to the light blue tube, and thrombin inhibition is heparin.

preguntas.pregunta: How is bleeding into the skin distinguished from simple redness (erythema)?
opciones: Bleeding into the skin does not blanch when pressed; erythema does
Bleeding into the skin blanches when pressed; erythema does not
Bleeding into the skin is always larger than 2 mm; erythema is smaller
Bleeding into the skin is warm to the touch; erythema is cool
preguntas.explicacion: Redness of the skin should not be mistaken for bleeding: areas of bleeding into the skin do not become paler when pressed, whereas the redness of erythema does. The same test defines a non-blanching spot: one that does not disappear after brief pressure. Size separates petechiae (under 2 mm) from purpura (over 2 mm), not bleeding from erythema.
preguntas.fuente: MedlinePlus, Medical Encyclopedia: Bleeding into the skin, Considerations

Lets it cool to 4 degrees for 60 minutes, which separates the sperm from the seminal plasma
Measures the volume and the pH first, before any liquefaction has been allowed to occur
Divides it into three numbered tubes, one each for count, motility and morphology

opciones: A 70% alcohol swab for 30 seconds, then let it dry completely, about 30 seconds
A 70% alcohol swab for 30 seconds, then insert the needle at once while the skin is still wet
Povidone iodine for 30 seconds, since it disinfects better than alcohol before a routine draw
A 70% alcohol swab kept wet for 10 minutes, the contact time given for bleach
preguntas.explicacion: Step 5 gives the numbers: a 70% alcohol swab applied for 30 seconds, then complete drying, which takes about 30 seconds more. Nails may be any length as long as gloves are worn for every patient contact
preguntas.explicacion: Natural nails should not extend past the fingertip, and artificial nails or extensions should not be worn when in direct contact with high-risk patients; it also notes that skin under rings carries more germs. StatPearls adds that long or artificial nails have been linked to outbreaks in intensive care and surgical settings, that current guidance keeps nails under 0.5 cm, and that nails should be free of polish and artificial coverings. Gloves do not cancel these rules, since they are not a substitute for hand hygiene.

preguntas.pregunta: An add-on for a viral RNA test is requested on an EDTA whole blood tube that has been in the refrigerator for two days. Under the general stability guidelines for whole blood, can it be used?
opciones: No: whole blood at 2 to 8 °C is listed as acceptable for RNA targets for only about 4 hours, though DNA holds 72 hours
Yes: whole blood at 2 to 8 °C is listed as acceptable for RNA targets for 72 hours, the same period given for DNA
Yes: EDTA whole blood is stable for RNA targets at 2 to 8 °C for 5 days, the figure the guideline gives for plasma
No: whole blood is never acceptable for RNA targets; only serum stored for 2 to 7 days at 2 to 8 °C can be used
preguntas.explicacion: The general guideline for whole blood gives room temperature for 24 hours and 2 to 8 °C for 72 hours when DNA is the target, but only 4 hours at 2 to 8 °C for RNA, with EDTA or ACD as the additives; plasma is the specimen listed at 2 to 8 °C for 5 days and serum for 2 to 7 days. When RNA is the target the recommendation is a tube with an RNA-stabilising reagent, so a two-day-old EDTA tube fails the add-on.

preguntas.pregunta: Blood is flowing well into the tubes. When does the WHO say the tourniquet should be released?
opciones: Before the needle is withdrawn, once enough blood has been collected
After the needle is withdrawn, while gentle pressure is applied with clean gauze
After it has been in place for two minutes, even if more tubes remain to be filled
As soon as the needle enters the vein, before any blood flow is established
preguntas.explicacion: Step 6 is explicit: once sufficient blood has been collected, the tourniquet comes off BEFORE the needle is withdrawn; the gauze and gentle pressure come after the needle is out. The guideline adds that some other guidelines go further and recommend removing it as soon as blood flow is established, and in any case before two minutes have passed with it in place. Two minutes is therefore a ceiling, not the moment to release, and before flow is established is earlier than any guideline the WHO cites.
preguntas.fuente: WHO, Guidelines on Drawing Blood: Best Practices in Phlebotomy (2010), Section 2.2.3, Step 6: Take blood

preguntas.pregunta: A very low birth weight infant (under 1500 g) is in its second week of intensive care. What is typical of its cumulative phlebotomy loss?
opciones: It often equals or exceeds the infant's circulating blood volume, driving anemia of prematurity and transfusions
It rarely exceeds 5% of circulating volume, because microtiter tubes keep each draw below 0.5 mL
It is replaced within days by the infant's own erythropoiesis, so transfusion is seldom required
It is limited by law to 3 mL per kilogram per day in every neonatal unit in the United States
preguntas.explicacion: Phlebotomy losses are a significant contributor to anemia in very low birth weight infants, with cumulative loss during the first weeks often equaling or exceeding circulating blood volume, strongly correlated with transfusion. In one such unit more than half of the infants' blood volume had been drawn for testing; a reduction program lowered blood out from 18.1 to 15.0 mL/kg over 3 weeks.

preguntas.pregunta: A patient wants to cancel an authorization she signed to release her records to her employer. How may she revoke it under HIPAA?
opciones: In writing at any time, except for actions already taken in reliance on it
Only before the covered entity has received and acted on the request
Orally at any time, and the covered entity must recall records already sent
Not until the expiration date or event stated on the form has passed
preguntas.explicacion: Section 164.508(b)(5) lets an individual revoke an authorization at any time, provided the revocation is in writing; the exceptions are actions the covered entity has already taken in reliance on the authorization, and certain insurance situations where other law gives the insurer a right to contest a claim. Records already sent cannot be recalled by the revocation, but no further disclosures may be made under it. An authorization whose expiration has passed or that is known to be revoked is defective and cannot be used.

preguntas.pregunta: How are sharp instruments passed in a procedure room so that two people are not put at risk at once?
opciones: Through a neutral zone, so the device is never handed person to person
By the person who used it, who announces the pass before letting go
With the tip capped by hand, which is allowed whenever a device is passed
Inside the sharps container, which is carried between the two workers
preguntas.explicacion: Operating rooms and other procedural areas use a standardized neutral zone, or hands-free passing technique, so that the instrument is set down and picked up instead of travelling from one hand to another. Handing and passing devices during or after use accounts for about a tenth of hollow-bore needle injuries in surveillance hospitals, and collisions with a coworker for another eight percent. Capping a used needle by hand is prohibited unless no alternative is feasible.
preguntas.fuente: StatPearls, "Needlestick", Introduction; NIOSH, Alert 2000-108, Figure 2

preguntas.pregunta: A parent asks why the nurse called the heel stick 'the PKU test'. What is true of that name?
opciones: It is no longer accurate, because the screen now checks for many conditions beyond PKU
It is the official name, because phenylketonuria is the one condition every state must screen for first
It is accurate only in two-screen states, where the second card tests for PKU alone
It refers to the pulse oximetry part of screening, not to the blood spots
preguntas.explicacion: Blood spot screening is sometimes called the heel stick or the 24-hour test; although some providers still call it the PKU test, the term is no longer accurate because newborn screening now checks for many conditions. Screening began in the 1960s with Dr Guthrie's blood test for PKU. The name survives only as habit.

Draw a non-additive tube first and discard it in every case
Draw a red clot activator tube first to prime the needle
Draw two light blue tubes and discard the first one
preguntas.explicacion: Footnote d of Table 2.3 says that when a routine coagulation assay is the only test, one light blue tube alone may be collected. The plain tube drawn ahead of it is an option reserved for the case in which contamination by tissue fluids or thromboplastins is a concern; it is not a rule for every draw. Neither a red tube nor a duplicate citrate tube is mentioned as a primer.

opciones: Yes; the table is given for vacuum tubes or syringe and needle, so citrate, SST, EDTA
No; once the blood is already in the syringe, additive carry-over is no longer possible
Yes, but reversed, so the EDTA tube that needs a full draw is filled first
No; with a syringe the largest tube is always filled first to protect the vacuum
preguntas.explicacion: Step 8 presents Table 2.3 as the recommended order for vacuum tubes or for syringe and needle, so the same sequence is followed when transferring: citrate (3), serum separator (5), EDTA (8). preguntas.pregunta: What does a reticulocyte count estimate, and what proportion of the red cells should reticulocytes normally be?
opciones: The rate of red cell production; about 1 to 2 percent of erythrocytes
The rate of platelet production; about 2 to 4 percent of formed elements
The share of immature neutrophils; about 2 to 8 percent of leukocytes
The share of red cells being hemolyzed; less than 1 percent of the count
preguntas.explicacion: A reticulocyte is an erythrocyte in its first day or two in the circulation, still carrying remnants of organelles. Reticulocytes should be about 1 to 2 percent of the erythrocyte count, and that share serves as a rough gauge of how fast red cells are being produced; abnormally low or high values point to a production problem. Immature neutrophils are called bands, a different measure.

preguntas.pregunta: An uncircumcised man is handed a clean-catch kit. What is the first cleaning step he should be told to perform?
opciones: Pull back the foreskin, then clean the head of the penis with a sterile wipe
Clean the head of the penis with a sterile wipe, leaving the foreskin in place
Wash the tip of the penis downward with soap and water, as for an infant
Wipe the urethral opening twice, front to back, with two separate wipes
preguntas.explicacion: The male instruction is to clean the head of the penis with a sterile wipe, and a man who is not circumcised has to retract the foreskin first so the wipe reaches the glans. Leaving the foreskin in place defeats the cleaning. Soap-and-water washing from the tip downward is the infant routine, and the two front-to-back wipes are the female instruction. He then voids a little into the toilet, stops, and collects until the cup is half full.

preguntas.pregunta: A laboratory with a 4 % hemolysis rate wants to know where it stands. What did the survey of 772 laboratories report?
opciones: Most of them, 71 %, stayed under 3 %, and 15 % fell between 3 % and 6 %
Most of them, 71 %, stayed under 1 %, and 15 % fell between 1 % and 3 %
Most of them exceeded 6 %, with emergency samples pulling the average up
Most of them clustered near 10 %, the figure reported for emergency rooms
preguntas.explicacion: In that survey 71 % of the laboratories had a hemolysis rate below 3 % and 15 % fell between 3 % and 6 %, with the highest values coming from emergency department specimens. A separate report put emergency samples at 10 % to 30 %. A laboratory at 4 % therefore sits in the upper range, which the authors of one such laboratory explained by their neonatal and emergency workload.

preguntas.pregunta: A tube reaches the lab with a label for the wrong patient. The unit calls and asks the technician to print a new label and stick it over the old one. What does good practice say?
opciones: Relabeling by laboratory, clinical staff or third parties is strongly discouraged; a new specimen is collected
Relabeling is acceptable if the nurse who drew the specimen confirms the patient's identity by telephone with the unit
Relabeling is acceptable when it is done by laboratory personnel and documented in the record system
Relabeling is acceptable for hematology tubes but never for specimens intended for blood bank testing
preguntas.explicacion: Laboratories are expected to have a clear procedure for unlabeled and mislabeled specimens, and relabeling, whoever does it, is strongly discouraged: once the link between patient and tube is lost, a telephone confirmation or a documented note cannot restore it. A mislabeled tube is a misidentification, which is associated with the worst clinical outcomes, so the safe course is a new specimen. There is no exception by test type.

preguntas.pregunta: During a clean-catch collection, at what point should the patient start filling the cup?
opciones: After voiding a small amount into the toilet and stopping, then collecting until the cup is about half full
As soon as the stream begins, collecting the first portion until the cup is about half full
After voiding a small amount into the toilet, then collecting every drop until the bladder is empty
After the stream has ended, collecting the last portion that remains and filling the cup to the top
preguntas.explicacion: The patient voids a small amount into the toilet, stops the flow, holds the cup a few inches from the urethra and fills it to about half, then finishes voiding into the toilet. The first portion carries the most contaminating cells and bacteria, which is why it is discarded; collecting every drop is the rule for a timed collection and for semen, not for a midstream sample. About 15 to 30 mL is enough for analysis, so the cup is never filled to the top.

Light blue, light green PST, serum separator, purple EDTA
Purple EDTA, light blue, serum separator, light green PST

More pain than expected, and clotting inside the citrate tube
A mislabelled specimen, and possible injury to a nerve nearby
A short draw in the grey tube, and bruising around the site

preguntas.pregunta: A donor hands over a container with about 30 mL of urine. What does the collector do?
opciones: Discard it and begin a second collection with a new container and the same form
Pour the 30 mL into bottle A and leave bottle B empty for a later collection
Send it as an insufficient specimen and let the laboratory decide what to do
Keep it and ask the donor to add to the same container after drinking water
preguntas.explicacion: Below 45 mL the specimen is discarded and a second collection begins immediately, using a new collection container and the same chain of custody form; temperature and physical characteristics are checked again on the second one. preguntas.pregunta: The order reads 'liver function tests' with no note about fasting. When does that group call for a fast?
opciones: In some cases, for instance when ordered as part of a metabolic panel
Always, because liver enzymes climb sharply after any meal is eaten
Never, because liver enzymes are not affected by food or by drink
Only when the patient also takes medicines that act on the liver
preguntas.explicacion: Liver function tests sit on the list of tests a patient may also be asked to fast for, alongside the renal function panel. Where the form is silent, the provider is asked.

preguntas.pregunta: A first-run potassium on an inpatient comes back far above the laboratory's critical limit. According to the published guidance on critical limits, what happens before the physician is called?
opciones: The value is confirmed by a second determination in the same sample, and a senior laboratory member verifies it
A new specimen is drawn by venipuncture, since the first tube is assumed to be hemolysed or contaminated
The result is released to the chart at once; confirmation is done only if the physician questions the value
The sample is recentrifuged and re-run on a second analyzer to rule out an instrument error before release
preguntas.explicacion: A critical result is not reported to the treating physician until it has been confirmed by a second determination in the same sample, and a senior laboratory member, such as the laboratory doctor, clinical chemist or senior technologist, verifies it and discusses it with the clinician. Preanalytical influences, like glucose drawn through a catheter used for a glucose infusion, are a frequent source of seemingly critical values, and those are cleared up by testing another, properly collected sample.

preguntas.pregunta: Which control does OSHA suggest for a phlebotomist who sorts specimens at a bench for hours at a stretch?
opciones: Rotate tasks; provide an adjustable bench with knee room and a chair with a footrest
Provide a back belt and require two-person lifts for every full specimen rack
Limit sorting to 20 minutes per shift and assign the rest to housekeeping
Install anti-fatigue mats and require standing for the whole shift
preguntas.explicacion: The recognized controls for laboratory musculoskeletal hazards include automated specimen delivery systems to cut reaching and repetition, supportive chairs with footrests, adjustable workstations with enough knee clearance so the knees do not hit the bench, rotating tasks or limiting time on them, ergonomic computer stations for sitting and standing, anti-fatigue mats for standing stations, and handling devices for heavy carboys. Mats help where standing is unavoidable but do not justify standing all shift, and back belts are not among the listed controls.

preguntas.pregunta: A nurse asks you to hand her supplies while she flushes a patient's multi-lumen central catheter. What is the routine she is following?

Flush every day, choosing a different lumen order each time, with saline
Flush once a week, each lumen in the same order, with heparin only
Flush before every blood draw only, using the largest lumen first
preguntas.explicacion: Central venous catheters are flushed every day to prevent clotting and keep them clear of blood, each lumen is flushed in the same order every time, and the solution is heparin or saline depending on the type of catheter. It stays tight from the first puncture until the last tube has been filled
It is removed for good once the flashback appears in the chamber
It is moved down the forearm below the cannula before the tubes are filled

preguntas.pregunta: A patient is about to give a saliva specimen for a molecular test and has just finished a coffee and brushed his teeth. Why does the collection instruction usually ask for a waiting period?
opciones: Food, non-water drinks, oral hygiene products and tobacco introduce substances that inhibit the molecular assay
Food and drink dilute the saliva so that its volume no longer reaches the minimum the collection device needs
Toothpaste raises the pH of saliva, which the assay reads as a positive result for most respiratory viruses
Coffee stains the collection swab, which blocks the optical reading of the amplification curve on the instrument
preguntas.explicacion: Saliva and buccal samples are normally collected only after a defined interval without food, non-water beverages, oral hygiene products or tobacco, because ingested material carries substances that interfere with molecular techniques, mainly polysaccharides, glycogen, enzymes such as the plasmin in milk products, and minerals such as calcium. In one study of children, interference from food was minimal when saliva was collected 20 minutes after a meal; the manufacturer's instructions fix the interval that applies.

A test performed by a physician or midlevel practitioner during a patient visit
A test that a laboratory chooses not to perform and refers to an accredited laboratory
A test of moderate complexity that has been exempted from proficiency testing
preguntas.explicacion: The definitions in 42 CFR 493.2 describe a waived test as a test system, assay or examination that HHS has determined meets the CLIA statutory criteria for waiver under section 353(d)(3) of the Public Health Service Act; everything else is a nonwaived test, of moderate or high complexity. Tests done by a physician, midlevel practitioner or dentist during a visit describe the provider-performed microscopy subcategory, which has its own certificate. preguntas.pregunta: A light blue citrate tube for a PT/INR comes back only about half full. What is the fill requirement for this tube, and why is a half-filled tube a problem?
opciones: Filling to at least 90% of the tube volume, to keep the 9:1 blood-to-citrate ratio
Filling to at least 50% of the tube volume, so that the 9:1 ratio is still within range
Filling to at least 90% of the tube volume, to keep the 1:9 blood-to-citrate ratio
Filling to the line only when the patient's hematocrit is above 55 percent
preguntas.explicacion: The tube has to be filled to within 90% of its full volume so that blood and sodium citrate stay in a 9 to 1 ratio; a half-filled tube breaks that ratio. The coagulopathies review adds that underfilling, like a hematocrit above 55%, raises the relative citrate level and disturbs the recalcification step of the assay. The ratio is nine parts blood to one of citrate, not the reverse.

preguntas.pregunta: How does a self re-sheathing needle and syringe protect the worker?

A spring pulls the used needle back inside the syringe barrel
A hinged cap is snapped shut over the bevel with both hands
A blunt inner cannula slides out ahead of the sharpened tip
preguntas.explicacion: In this design a sleeve is moved forward over the needle, forming a guard around the used tip and preventing the device being used again. Retraction into the syringe body is the mechanism of the manually retractable device, which is a different row of the same table.

preguntas.pregunta: A fasting patient asks whether she may sip water on the way in. Why is she still encouraged to drink plain water?
opciones: Water keeps more fluid in the veins, which eases getting the sample
Water dilutes the sample, which lowers a falsely raised glucose
Water shortens the fast needed from twelve hours down to eight
Water clears the stomach so the fast counts from that moment on
preguntas.explicacion: Plain water is the one thing allowed during a fast; juice, coffee, soda and flavoured carbonated water are not, since they enter the bloodstream and affect results. Staying well hydrated makes the testing process a little easier, because water helps hold more fluid in the veins and so makes the sample easier to obtain.

preguntas.pregunta: A patient's forearm shows no vein joining the cephalic and basilic veins at the elbow. Which pattern of the cubital fossa is that?
opciones: Type IV, in which no communicating branch links the two veins
Type II, in which the median cubital vein links the two veins
Type I, in which the median antebrachial vein links both veins
Type III, in which the median cubital vein is unusually large
preguntas.explicacion: The superficial veins here fall into four patterns. Type IV is the one with no communicating branch between cephalic and basilic; type II, where the median cubital vein joins them, is the commonest, followed by type I with a dominant median antebrachial vein. Type III has a poorly developed vein.

preguntas.pregunta: A newborn's CRP is ordered to monitor for perinatal infection and the serum returns a hemolysis index of about 800 µmol/L. What does the laboratory do with the CRP?
opciones: Rejects it and asks for a repeat sample, since an index above about 622 µmol/L can underestimate CRP
Reports it, since specific proteins such as CRP are immune to hemolysis interference at any index
Reports it with a note, since only indices above 2,000 µmol/L are considered severe in newborns
Dilutes the serum to bring the index below 31 µmol/L and reports the CRP measured on the dilution
preguntas.explicacion: Specific proteins are less sensitive to hemolysis than many chemistry tests, but severe in vitro hemolysis can still interfere: a hemolysis index above 622 µmol/L may cause underestimation of CRP, and in that series 199 newborn CRP requests were rejected for severe hemolysis, the highest index being 1,997 µmol/L. Each rejected CRP became reliable after the blood sampling was repeated two to five hours later. The 31 µmol/L figure is merely the index equivalent of 0.5 g/L free haemoglobin, the threshold that defines a hemolysed sample.
preguntas.fuente: PMC, "Detection of haemolysis, a frequent preanalytical problem in the serum of newborns and adults" (EJIFCC 2020, PMC7109500), Materials and Methods; Results and Table 2

preguntas.pregunta: During teach-back the patient says she will have coffee with sugar before the fasting draw. What is the next step?
opciones: Explain again using a different approach, then ask her to teach it back once more
Repeat the same words more slowly and then move on to the next topic
Have her read the instruction sheet aloud back to you, word for word
Record that she did not pass the teach-back and reschedule the test
preguntas.explicacion: When teach-back uncovers a misunderstanding, the clinician explains with a different approach and asks for teach-back again, repeating the cycle until the patient can describe the information correctly in their own words; parroting the words back, or reading the handout verbatim, does not show understanding. Teach-back is not a test that a patient fails.
preguntas.fuente: AHRQ, Health Literacy Universal Precautions Toolkit, Tool 5: Use the Teach-Back Method, Action

preguntas.pregunta: Where does a safety data sheet say how a chemical should be stored and which products it must be kept away from?
opciones: Section 7, which also gives the hygiene practices for handling it
Section 2, which also gives the classification and the signal word
Section 14, which also gives the shipping name and the UN number
Section 11, which also gives the toxicity figures and the symptoms
preguntas.explicacion: Section 7 is the day-to-day section: precautions for safe handling, including how to deal with incompatible chemicals, how to keep the product from being released, and general hygiene advice such as the ban on eating, drinking and smoking in work areas; and then the conditions for safe storage, incompatibilities and any specific requirement such as ventilation. Section 14, on transport, is one of the four sections OSHA does not enforce.

preguntas.pregunta: The FDA scores seven criteria to categorize a test system. What total makes the test moderate complexity?
opciones: A total of 12 or less across the seven scored criteria
A total of 14 or less across the seven scored criteria
A total of 12 or more across the seven scored criteria
A total of 7 or less across the seven scored criteria
preguntas.explicacion: Each of the seven scorecard criteria is graded 1, 2 or 3, with 1 the lowest level of complexity. The seven scores are added: 12 or less is moderate complexity, above 12 is high. Tests waived by regulation or cleared for home use are categorized as waived without scoring, and a test system that has not yet been categorized defaults to high complexity.
preguntas.fuente: FDA, CLIA Categorizations, What is a CLIA Categorization?

preguntas.pregunta: A biochemistry laboratory graded each of its quality failures twice, once for the harm actually done and once for the harm that could have been done. What pattern emerged?
opciones: Most scored lowest for actual harm, yet most scored highest for potential harm
Most scored highest for actual harm, and most scored highest for potential harm
Most scored lowest for actual harm, and most scored lowest for potential harm
Actual and potential scores matched, because every error was caught in time
preguntas.explicacion: In that grading exercise 72.7 % of the errors carried an actual adverse impact score of 1, the least severe grade, while 65.9 % carried a potential adverse impact score of 5, the most severe. Nearly nine out of ten of the errors were preanalytical. The gap is the point: most near misses do no harm this time, and the same near miss could do the worst harm next time.

preguntas.pregunta: A urine collection bag is being applied to a male infant. Where does the bag go?
opciones: The whole penis is placed inside the bag and the adhesive strip is pressed onto the skin around it
Only the tip of the penis is placed inside the bag and the adhesive strip is pressed onto the diaper
The bag is taped over the two folds of skin on either side of the opening where urine flows out
The bag is laid loose inside the diaper, without adhesive, so that the voided urine drains into it
preguntas.explicacion: For a boy the entire penis goes into the plastic bag and the sticky strip is attached to the skin; for a girl the bag is placed over the two folds of skin on either side of the vagina. Before the bag goes on, the area around the urethra is washed thoroughly with the soap or wipes the provider supplied. A bag that is not sealed to the skin, or one that only holds the tip, will leak.
preguntas.fuente: MedlinePlus, Medical Encyclopedia: Urine collection - infants (003417), How the Test is Performed

preguntas.pregunta: A patient arrives at the office laboratory out of breath after climbing several flights of stairs. What is recommended before the draw, and why?
opciones: Have the patient sit for at least 15 minutes, since posture changes alter biochemistry results
Draw immediately, because exertion raises the venous pressure and makes the veins easier to find
Have the patient lie down for two to three minutes and then draw with a butterfly set
Postpone the draw for 24 hours, the interval the chapter sets after physical activity
preguntas.explicacion: Patients in an office setting should stay seated for at least 15 minutes before the procedure, because statistically significant changes in several biochemistry parameters follow a change in position, and any unavoidable change should be recorded. The 24-hour rule in the same chapter concerns avoiding excessive physical activity before the collection, not a postponement.
preguntas.fuente: StatPearls, "Phlebotomy", section Preparation (patient position)

preguntas.pregunta: A patient who smells strongly of alcohol refuses his draw and the nurse is unsure how impaired he is. What is directed?
opciones: Carry out the usual capacity assessment, since intoxication varies in degree
Draw anyway, because intoxication always removes the right to refuse care
Accept the refusal with no assessment, since the refusal is his to make
Wait for a court order before any decision about the draw is taken
preguntas.explicacion: Patients under the influence of alcohol or drugs may lack capacity, and where there is uncertainty about the level of intoxication, the typical assessment of capacity is performed. That impairment is often temporary: once sober, the same patient may make sound decisions again. Formal guardianship through a court belongs to long-term situations.
preguntas.fuente: StatPearls, "Refusal of Care", section Issues of Concern, Intoxicated Patients

preguntas.pregunta: Pleural, peritoneal and synovial fluids have been aspirated for culture. How should they travel to the laboratory?
opciones: Promptly and at room temperature, which keeps the organisms viable
Promptly and refrigerated, which keeps the organisms viable in transit
Promptly and frozen, since the cell count is read from the thawed fluid
Whenever convenient, provided each container has been sealed and labeled
preguntas.explicacion: These fluids are aspirated aseptically into sterile containers, and their appearance, color, turbidity, viscosity and any clots are recorded. Portions go for cell count and differential, for protein and glucose, for culture and for cytology. For the microbiology portion, prompt transport at room temperature is what keeps the organisms alive, the same principle that governs cerebrospinal fluid.
preguntas.fuente: StatPearls, "Overview of the Ordering and Evaluation of Laboratory Tests", Body Fluid Samples

preguntas.pregunta: Under which measure was the Institutional Review Board established in the United States?
opciones: The National Research Act, in 1974
The National Research Act, in 1984
The Belmont Report, issued in 1976
The Declaration of Helsinki revisions
preguntas.explicacion: The board was established in 1974 under the National Research Act, which brought in regulations for human research after unethical practices such as the Tuskegee syphilis experiments. The Belmont Report sets out respect for persons, beneficence and justice as guiding principles, and the Declaration of Helsinki is an ethical statement; neither created the board.

preguntas.pregunta: A fingerstick A1C on a clinic's point-of-care analyzer reads 6.6 % in a patient without a diabetes diagnosis. What should happen next?
opciones: The result is confirmed with a venous sample before any diagnosis, because capillary point-of-care A1C values are variable
Diabetes is diagnosed on the spot, because 6.5 % or higher on any A1C method is diagnostic without a second test
The fingerstick is repeated the same day and the two capillary results are averaged to reach the diagnostic value
The patient is scheduled for a repeat fingerstick A1C in three months, and diabetes is diagnosed if it is still 6.5 % or more
preguntas.explicacion: Because capillary point-of-care A1C testing is variable, any A1C obtained from a capillary sample should be confirmed with a venous sample before a diagnosis is made; point-of-care devices also tend to read about 0.5 % lower than laboratory assays. For screening and diagnosis, point-of-care A1C is restricted to FDA-approved devices run in CLIA-certified laboratories performing moderate complexity or higher testing, with certified methods.
preguntas.fuente: StatPearls, "Hemoglobin A1C", section Specimen Requirements and Procedure; Diagnostic Tests; StatPearls, "Blood Glucose Monitoring", section Quality Control and Lab Safety

preguntas.pregunta: Which superficial vein connects the cephalic and basilic veins in the cubital fossa?
opciones: The median cubital vein
The median antebrachial vein
The brachial vein
The dorsal venous arch
preguntas.explicacion: As the cephalic and basilic veins approach the cubital fossa they become joined by the median cubital vein, which has a median cephalic and a median basilic connection. The dorsal venous arch is where both veins begin on the back of the hand, the median antebrachial vein is the dominant vessel only in the type I fossa, and the brachial vein is deep.
preguntas.fuente: StatPearls, "Anatomy, Shoulder and Upper Limb, Veins", section Structure and Function

preguntas.pregunta: What does the regulation say about preparing the donor's skin and collecting the unit?
opciones: Prepare it for maximum assurance of a sterile container, and collect aseptically
Prepare it with a single 70% alcohol swab, and collect into a vented open system
Prepare it with a non-alcoholic antiseptic, as for a blood alcohol collection
Prepare it with the same swab used to draw the pre-donation screening sample
preguntas.explicacion: The skin at the phlebotomy site is prepared thoroughly and carefully by a method that gives maximum assurance of a sterile container of blood, and the blood is collected by aseptic methods in a sterile system, closed or vented so long as the vent protects against contamination. Non-alcoholic antiseptic is the rule for a blood alcohol specimen, a different problem entirely.

preguntas.pregunta: At which blood glucose level is a patient considered to be hypoglycemic?
opciones: Below 70 mg/dL (3.9 mmol/L), which can already do harm
Below 100 mg/dL (5.6 mmol/L), the lower end of the fasting range
Below 55 mg/dL (3.1 mmol/L), and never above that figure
Below 40 mg/dL (2.2 mmol/L), when the patient loses consciousness
preguntas.explicacion: A blood sugar under 70 mg/dL, or 3.9 mmol/L, counts as low and can be harmful at or below that level. Symptoms may not appear until the glucose falls below 55 mg/dL, which is why the number matters and not only how the patient looks. Severe low blood sugar that ends in unconsciousness is what is called insulin shock.
preguntas.fuente: MedlinePlus, "Low blood sugar", Overview

preguntas.pregunta: The preparation a test requires cannot be met for a particular patient. How does the ordering guidance describe that?
opciones: As a contraindication, alongside results that will not alter management
As a rejection criterion applied once the specimen reaches the laboratory
As an interfering factor, noted in the comment field beside the result
As a postanalytical problem, handled when the report is interpreted
preguntas.explicacion: Contraindications are said to arise when results will not alter management, when testing imposes unnecessary harm, or when preanalytical requirements cannot be met. Whether a specimen is acceptable is judged later, and the postanalytical phase covers verification, interpretation, documentation and communication of the results.
preguntas.fuente: StatPearls, "Overview on Ordering and Evaluation of Laboratory Tests", section Continuing Education Activity and section Testing Procedures

preguntas.pregunta: Where should the needle enter the skin when performing venipuncture on an immobilized infant?
opciones: 3 to 5 mm distal to the vein, so the vein is not pushed away
Directly over the vein, so the needle enters on the first pass
3 to 5 mm proximal to the vein, so the needle tip travels with the flow
1 cm distal to the vein, the width the alcohol swab must cover
preguntas.explicacion: Once the infant or child is immobilized, the skin is punctured 3 to 5 mm distal to, that is away from, the vein, because this allows good access without pushing the vein away. If the needle ends up alongside the vein rather than in it, withdraw it slightly without removing it and angle it into the vessel. Blood is then drawn slowly and steadily.

preguntas.pregunta: What concentration of sodium citrate does the light blue coagulation tube contain?
preguntas.explicacion: Both the tube collection review and the prothrombin time chapter give 3.2% sodium citrate as the anticoagulant of the light blue tube. The figure 9 comes from a different rule in the same chapter, the 9 to 1 ratio of blood to citrate that the tube must keep, and the other two numbers are misplacements of the decimal point. The citrate works by chelating calcium.

preguntas.pregunta: A clinician takes a telephone consult about a named patient from the phone in the hospital cafeteria. What is wrong with that?
opciones: The talk is allowed, but it has to happen away from the public
The talk is barred, since consults require written authorization
The talk is allowed only if the patient is on the line as well
The talk is barred, because phone lines are never encrypted
preguntas.explicacion: Consulting another provider is a permitted conversation; where it takes place is what matters. Such conversations are to be held away from the public and in private rooms, and a telephone consult from a cafeteria line, where others can hear, is the example given of how not to do it. Staff may still coordinate verbally at a nurses' station, and providers may discuss a patient's status by telephone.

preguntas.pregunta: When does the CDC say soap and water must be used rather than alcohol-based hand sanitizer?
opciones: When hands are visibly soiled, after using the restroom, or during C. difficile outbreaks
Before every aseptic task and after any contact with the patient's immediate surroundings
Whenever the sanitizer on hand contains less than 60 percent alcohol by volume
Whenever gloves have been worn for longer than the 20 seconds a hand rub takes
preguntas.explicacion: The CDC prefers alcohol-based hand sanitizer in most clinical situations unless hands are visibly soiled, and reserves soap and water for visibly soiled hands, before eating, after using the restroom, and during care of patients with suspected or confirmed infection in outbreaks of C. difficile and norovirus. StatPearls explains that spore-forming and non-enveloped organisms resist alcohol, so mechanical removal by washing is needed. Aseptic tasks and contact with surroundings are moments for hand hygiene by either method, not reasons to choose soap.

preguntas.pregunta: The superficial veins of the cubital fossa are classified into four types. Which pattern is the most common?
opciones: Type II, in which the median cubital vein joins the cephalic and basilic veins (the M pattern)
Type I, in which a dominant median antebrachial vein joins both veins (the N pattern)
Type III, in which the brachial cephalic vein is poorly developed or missing
Type IV, in which there is no communicating branch between cephalic and basilic
preguntas.explicacion: Type II, with the cephalic and basilic veins connected by the median cubital vein and also called type M, is the most common pattern, followed by type I, the N type with a dominant median antebrachial vein. It adds that because of this variation, bruising, hematoma and sensory changes from mispuncture have been reported across health systems.

preguntas.pregunta: How is a spot tested to decide whether it is non-blanching?
opciones: Brief pressure is applied, and the spot does not disappear
Brief pressure is applied, and the spot fades then returns
The skin is stretched, and the spot spreads sideways with it
The skin is cooled, and the spot pales under the cold pack
preguntas.explicacion: A non-blanching spot is one that stays visible after brief pressure is put on the area. That single manoeuvre separates bleeding into the skin, which does not pale, from simple redness of the skin, which does. Both petechiae and purpura are defined as non-blanching.

preguntas.pregunta: A laboratory starts logging every preanalytical incident in one simple shared program instead of on paper notes. What does the literature credit that with achieving?
opciones: It harmonises incident reporting, which is otherwise commonly left undone
It removes the need for a written procedure covering unacceptable specimens
It shortens turnaround time by routing the rejected samples automatically
It covers the proficiency testing requirement for the preanalytical phase
preguntas.explicacion: Incidents in the preanalytical phase are commonly underreported, so the numbers a laboratory holds understate the problem. A simple and freely available program for recording those errors systematically was shown to be worthwhile precisely because it makes reporting comparable within one laboratory and even between laboratories in different countries.

preguntas.pregunta: A cerebrospinal fluid specimen from a neurology ICU arrives in a urine cup instead of a sterile CSF tube. How does the emergency laboratory handle it?
opciones: A laboratory medicine specialist decides whether this precious specimen is rejected or accepted
The accessioning clerk rejects it automatically, as with any specimen in an improper container
It is accepted without review, because CSF can never be recollected from the same patient
It is transferred by the clerk into a sterile tube and processed as an ordinary specimen
preguntas.explicacion: Improper container is a standing rejection criterion, and sending CSF in a urine cup is described as a common mistake in the neurology ICU; but for precious specimens such as CSF, bone marrow or aspirates received in unsuitable tubes or under wrong transport conditions, the decision to reject or accept is reserved to the laboratory medicine specialists rather than made automatically at the desk.

preguntas.pregunta: Which disadvantage does the WHO device table attach to collecting blood with a hypodermic needle and syringe?
opciones: The blood has to be transferred, adding needle-stick and splash risk
It cannot be used for blood drawing in the paediatric population
It cannot be heparinized, so it is unsuitable for arterial blood samples
It requires more training than an evacuated tube system
preguntas.explicacion: Table C.1 lists as disadvantages of the syringe that it requires blood transfer, creating additional risk of needle-stick injuries or blood splashing, that large or multiple samples are difficult, and that a smaller syringe and paediatric tube are needed for children. preguntas.pregunta: A patient says the only thing taken that morning before a fasting draw was a cup of black coffee, no sugar. Under the guidance on fasting samples, is the specimen acceptable?
opciones: No: during the fasting period water is acceptable, but coffee and other drinks such as energy drinks are not allowed
Yes: black coffee without sugar adds no calories and is treated the same way as plain water during a fast
Yes, provided the coffee was taken more than 2 hours before the draw and the patient then drank plain water
No: coffee is allowed only together with the morning medicines, which this patient did not take
preguntas.explicacion: Morning sampling after a fast of at least 12 hours since the last solid meal is the recommended condition; water during the fasting period is acceptable, but other drinks, coffee and energy drinks included, are not allowed on the morning of the procedure, and alcohol is avoided for the 24 hours before. Non-fasting samples are accepted only for patients who cannot tolerate the fast, for emergencies and for parameters that fasting does not affect; fasting status is double-checked once identification is verified.

preguntas.pregunta: A refrigerator that stores patient samples and control materials is typically kept in which temperature range?
preguntas.explicacion: The usual sample refrigerator runs between 2 and 8 °C, a sample freezer between −25 and −15 °C, and rooms used for testing and storage between 15 and 30 °C. The correct range for any unit is ultimately set by the acceptable storage range in the manufacturer's instructions for what is kept in it. Temperatures are checked and recorded daily, and the testing room before it is used, whatever monitoring device is installed.

Draw from the right hand only, never from the antecubital fossa
Draw from either arm, as long as the tourniquet stays under one minute

preguntas.pregunta: A volunteer blood donation center decides gloves are not routinely needed for every draw. What must the employer still do?

Record every draw done without gloves in the sharps injury log kept for the year
Obtain a signed declination from each employee who draws without wearing gloves

preguntas.explicacion: Paragraph (d)(3)(ix)(D) lets a volunteer blood donation center judge that routine gloving for every phlebotomy is unnecessary, but it attaches four duties: reevaluate that judgment periodically, make gloves available to anyone who wants them, do nothing to discourage their use, and require them when the employee has cuts or breaks in the skin, when hand contamination looks likely, and while the employee is being trained. preguntas.pregunta: How should paper records and prescription labels that contain PHI be disposed of?
opciones: Shredded or incinerated so that nobody can piece them back together
Placed in a red biohazard bag and treated as regulated waste
Handed to the person in charge of shredding to take home and destroy later
Kept in a locked cabinet indefinitely, since PHI may never be destroyed
preguntas.explicacion: Documents with PHI are shredded or incinerated so that no reconstruction is possible, computers, CDs and drives are completely erased before disposal, and the people assigned to destruction are chosen so that records are in fact destroyed rather than taken home; letting the shredding staff carry records home is exactly what that selection is meant to prevent. A red bag is the container for regulated waste under the bloodborne pathogens standard, which is about infection, not confidentiality, and HIPAA sets a retention period for its own documentation rather than a ban on destroying records.

Any tube, as long as each one is labeled with the test it is meant for

preguntas.pregunta: After a needlestick, what does the CDC say about squeezing the wound or applying bleach to it?
opciones: Neither has evidence behind it, and caustic agents like bleach are not advised
Squeezing is recommended to expel contaminated blood; bleach is not advised
Bleach at a 1:10 dilution is recommended on the wound; squeezing is not
Both are recommended right away, before the wound is washed with soap and water
preguntas.explicacion: No scientific evidence shows that using antiseptics or squeezing the wound reduces the risk of transmitting a bloodborne pathogen, and a caustic agent such as bleach is not recommended. The recommended care is washing the needlestick with soap and water. WHO's annex on occupational exposure agrees: wash with soap and water, no alcohol or strong disinfectant, let the wound bleed freely, and do not dress it. The 1:10 bleach dilution is for surfaces after a spill, never for skin.

The name on the wristband matches the name printed on the requisition

Inpatients only, because their meals are already controlled by the ward
Patients on therapeutic drug monitoring, who must eat together with the dose

preguntas.pregunta: What is the wall of a capillary made of, and what is the capillary's job?
opciones: One endothelial layer on a basement membrane; exchange with tissue fluid
Three tunics with a thin muscular media; regulation of blood pressure
Endothelium plus a thin layer of muscle cells; the main site of diapedesis
Rings of smooth muscle called sphincters; control of flow into the bed
preguntas.explicacion: The capillary wall is an endothelial layer surrounded by a basement membrane, sometimes a single cell wrapped around itself, and its function is perfusion: exchanging gases and other substances between blood and interstitial fluid. Capillaries are the smallest and most numerous vessels, built for exchange. Three tunics describe arterioles; sphincters belong to the metarteriole.

preguntas.pregunta: Why is the labeled-urea capsule for a 14C urea breath test swallowed whole rather than opened or chewed?
opciones: Because oral flora can carry urease, which would break the urea down in the mouth
Because the capsule shell is what delays gastric emptying long enough for the test
Because the radioactive dose is only safe if the isotope never touches the mucosa
Because chewing releases citric acid, which lowers the pH and slows the stomach
preguntas.explicacion: The test rests on urease, an enzyme absent from human cells, splitting urea into ammonia and carbon dioxide that is then breathed out. Bacteria in the mouth also carry urease, so the capsule goes down whole with lukewarm water to keep the reaction where it belongs. In the 13C version the mixture is drunk through a straw for the same reason, and citric acid is the test meal that slows gastric emptying.

preguntas.pregunta: A patient's venipuncture site keeps bleeding through the gauze after the draw. What is the most important first step?
opciones: Apply direct pressure over the site and keep it until the bleeding stops
Apply a tourniquet 2 to 3 inches above the site and note the time
Remove the soaked gauze, clean the wound, and apply fresh gauze
Raise the arm above the heart and peek every minute to check
preguntas.explicacion: Direct pressure is the most important step for external bleeding and stops most of it: press on the wound with a sterile bandage, clean cloth or, failing that, a hand, and maintain the pressure until the bleeding stops, without peeking. Raising the bleeding part can be added when possible, but checking every minute disturbs the clot. A soaked dressing is left in place with another on top, and a tourniquet is reserved for severe, life-threatening limb bleeding that continuous pressure has failed to control.

preguntas.pregunta: Why are veins preferred over arteries for a routine blood draw?
opciones: Veins run superficially, while arteries have thicker walls and more nerves, so puncturing them hurts more
Veins carry oxygenated blood, which is what most chemistry analysers are calibrated to measure
Arteries collapse under the vacuum of the tube, while veins tolerate the negative pressure
Arterial blood clots too quickly in a citrate tube to allow coagulation testing
preguntas.explicacion: Veins are preferred for efficiency and patient comfort because they run superficially, whereas arteries tend to have thicker walls and more associated nerves, making a puncture more painful; arterial sampling is reserved for arterial blood gases. preguntas.pregunta: What exactly is a platelet?
opciones: A fragment of megakaryocyte cytoplasm wrapped in plasma membrane
A small complete cell with a two-lobed nucleus, 8 to 10 µm wide
An immature erythrocyte that still contains remnants of organelles
A leukocyte that has left the circulation to phagocytize debris
preguntas.explicacion: A platelet is not a cell: it is a piece of the cytoplasm of a large marrow cell, the megakaryocyte, enclosed by a bit of plasma membrane, which is why the older name thrombocyte is misleading. Each megakaryocyte releases 2000 to 3000 platelets. The small two-lobed cell is the basophil, the immature red cell is the reticulocyte, and the emigrated phagocyte is the macrophage.

Sweep the nozzle from side to side across the flames

preguntas.pregunta: On a 75-g OGTT the 2-hour plasma glucose is 210 mg/dL. What does that result mean?

Impaired glucose tolerance, the range just below diabetes

preguntas.pregunta: Which three components must be present for a fire to ignite?
opciones: A fuel, an oxidizer like oxygen, and an ignition source
A fuel, a flammable liquid, and a compressed gas
Heat, smoke, and an electrical current from a wall outlet
Oxygen, nitrous oxide, and an electrocautery device
preguntas.explicacion: Three components are needed: a fuel source such as linens, flammable liquids or tissue; an oxidizer such as oxygen or nitrous oxide, which greatly increases combustibility; and an ignition source such as an open flame, electrostatic discharge, electrocautery, lasers or any energized device. The operating room is a high-risk setting because all three are usually present at once. Oxygen and nitrous oxide are both oxidizers and electrocautery is an ignition source, so that combination lacks a fuel; smoke is a product of fire, not a component.

Bend the arm firmly over the gauze and keep it tightly bent for at least five minutes
Lower the arm below the heart so the puncture seals under gravity
Rub the site through the gauze for 30 seconds to disperse any pooled blood
preguntas.explicacion: Step 6 says to withdraw the needle gently, apply gentle pressure with clean gauze or cotton wool, and ask the patient to hold it in place with the arm extended and raised; the patient is told not to bend the arm because doing so causes a haematoma. Lowering the arm and rubbing the site are not described anywhere in the guideline.
preguntas.fuente: WHO, Guidelines on Drawing Blood: Best Practices in Phlebotomy (2010), Section 2.2.3, Step 6: Take blood

preguntas.pregunta: A surgical hand scrub with an antimicrobial agent usually lasts how long?
opciones: About 2 to 6 minutes
About 15 to 20 seconds
About 10 to 15 minutes
About 30 to 60 seconds
preguntas.explicacion: Surgical antisepsis is a scrub that usually lasts 2 to 6 minutes; the clinical literature adds that scrubs of 10 minutes or more give no extra benefit and irritate the skin. The scrub is done with hands above the elbows, jewelry removed, nails cleaned under running water and a sterile brush or sponge, followed by drying with a sterile towel before sterile gloves. Fifteen to twenty seconds is routine handwashing, not surgical antisepsis.
